22.t: From Proto-Hellenic *gʷatiléus, with σ (s) developing by assibilation. Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀣𐀯𐀩𐀄 (qa-si-re-u), that is, *gʷasileus.

2.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kahi, from earlier *kasi, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥t-, from *ḱóm (“with”). Compare Hittite 𒃰𒋾 (kat-ti, “along with”).

38.t: From Proto-Hellenic *anḗr, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂nḗr. Cognates include Sanskrit नृ (nṛ́), नर॑ (nára), Latin neriosus and Old Irish nert.

26.t: Contraction of γαῖα (gaîă), from Proto-Hellenic *gaya, from a pre-Indo-European Pre-Greek substrate.

77.t: Probably from Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)ey, a locative form of *ís (“this”). See its sense, “that”, in ἐπεί (epeí) and compare the history of Latin sī.

43.t: First attested in Hellenic as Mycenaean Greek 𐀀𐀵𐀫𐀦 (a-to-ro-qo), of uncertain origin. Scholars used to consider it to be a compound from ἀνήρ (ănḗr, “man”) and ὤψ (ṓps, “face, appearance, look”): thus, "he who looks like a man".

7.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kúrios, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- (“to swell; to spread out; to be strong; to prevail”). By surface analysis, κῦρος (kûros, “supremacy”) + -ιος (-ĭos, adjective suffix).

20.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁s Proto-Indo-European *dʰh₁sós Proto-Hellenic *tʰehós Ancient Greek θεός From Proto-Hellenic *tʰehós (whence also Mycenaean Greek 𐀳𐀃 (te-o)), a thematicization of…

75.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hágiyos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁yáǵ-yo-s, from *h₁yaǵ- (“to sacrifice, worship”).

59.t: PIE word *swé Probably from Ancient Greek ἔθω (éthō, “I am accustomed, wont (to something)”) + -νος (-nos), equivalent to Proto-Indo-European *swedʰ-no-, expanded from the reflexive pronoun Proto-Indo-European *swé (“self”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”).

44.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-? Proto-Indo-European *-tḗr Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr Proto-Hellenic *patḗr Ancient Greek πατήρ From Proto-Hellenic *patḗr (compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀞𐀳 (pa-te)), from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.

48.t: From Proto-Hellenic *lógos, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to collect (words)”). See also λέγω (légō, “to reckon, say”).

95.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰōnā́, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoh₂-néh₂, from *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”) (whence φημί (phēmí, “to say, speak”)).

41.t: From Proto-Hellenic *ptólis, from Proto-Indo-European *tpólHis, from *tpelH- (“fortification; city”). The early form πτόλις (ptólis) shows metathesis tp > pt because Ancient Greek stop clusters always end in a coronal.

65.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mégas, from a conflation of Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s (“great”) with its derivative *meǵh₂los (“great”).

91.t: Traditionally derived from ὄψ (óps, “eye”) + θάλαμος (thálamos, “chamber”), but note the usual ancient Greek word for eye is the similar ὤψ (ṓps), with a long /o/.

62.t: By surface analysis, ψύχω (psū́khō, “to breathe, blow; to cool, chill; to dry”, verb) + -η (-ē, zero grade nominal suffix). The original meaning is thus supposed to have been breath.

28.t: Lengthened form of ἦμαρ (êmar, “day”). The initial aspiration ῾ (h) in Attic is probably by analogy with ἑσπέρα (hespérā).

58.t: From Proto-Hellenic *gʷənā. Cognates include the first element in Mycenaean Greek 𐀓𐀙𐀊 (ku-na-ja), Sanskrit ग्ना (gnā́), जनि॑ (jáni), Old Armenian կին (kin), and Old English cwēn (English queen).

69.t: Partial phono-semantic matching of Biblical Hebrew יְרוּשָׁלַיִם (Yərūšālayim) with ἱερός (hĭerós, “sacred; holy”).

94.t: Of disputed origin, with multiple theories proposed: * Perhaps from an older *(ϝ)ορσανός (*(w)orsanós), which may be related to οὐρέω (ouréō, “to urinate”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁worseye-, from *h₁wers- (“rain”) (compare Sanskrit वर्षति (varṣati, “it…

53.t: From Proto-Hellenic *akouhō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti, and cognate with English hear, hark and harken. In this word, the diphthong ου (ou) is genuine (see spurious diphthong on Wikipedia for an explanation).

99.t: Seemingly an inherited term, though the broad semantic range of the word makes ascertaining further origin and cognates difficult: * If from Proto-Indo-European *top-o-s: ** From Proto-Indo-European *tep- (“to hit, stick, smear”), and cognate with…

85.t: From Proto-Hellenic *údōr, from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (genitive *wednós (“of water”)), with ω (ō) from the plural), from the root *wed- (whence also ὕω (hū́ō, “to water, to let rain, to rain”)).

54.t: From *δισά (disá), from Proto-Indo-European *dwís (“twice, in two”) (related to δίς (dís, “twice”) and δύο (dúo, “two”)). Cognates include Latin dis- and Gothic 𐌳𐌹𐍃- (dis-).

13.t: From earlier υἱύς (huiús); see there for more.

74.t: From Proto-Indo-European *polh₁ús (“much, many”), o-grade derivative of the root *pleh₁- (“to fill”).

72.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pərai, apparently from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before, in front”) and/or *per- (identical meaning), the details of which are disputed. Compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀞𐀫 (pa-ro).

23.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʷoiwéyō, as shown by Doric/Aeolic ποιϝέω (poiwéō), perhaps derived from a noun *ποιϝός (*poiwós) (seen in many compounds as the suffix -ποιός (-poiós)), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoywós, from *kʷey- (“to pile, stow, gather”).

15.t: From Proto-Indo-European *próti, *préti. Cognates include Sanskrit प्रति (práti), Latin pretium, and Old Church Slavonic противъ (protivŭ).

80.t: From ϝέτος (wétos), from Proto-Hellenic *wétos, from Proto-Indo-European *wétos (“year”). Cognates include Latin vetus and Sanskrit वत्स (vatsá).

78.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hístāmi, from Proto-Indo-European *stísteh₂ti, the reduplicated present of *steh₂-.

29.t: Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀕𐀲 (me-ta); further derivation is uncertain.

93.t: From Egyptian ḥwt-kꜣ-ptḥ (literally “the temple of the ka of Ptah”), referring to Ptah’s temple in the important city of Memphis.

3.t: According to Beekes, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew (“again, away from”) + *to- (“that”); compare Proto-Germanic *auþijaz (“barren, empty”).

14.t: From Proto-Hellenic *dḗ, from Proto-Indo-European *de (deictic particle). See also δή (dḗ).

5.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tú, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. Cognates include Sanskrit त्वम् (tvam), Latin tū, Persian تو (to) and Old English þū (English thou).

31.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *légō, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to collect, gather”). Cognates include Latin legō and Albanian mbledh.

10.t: From Proto-Hellenic *ehmi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésmi (“to be, to exist”). Cognate with Old English eom (whence English am), Latin sum, Sanskrit अस्मि॑ (ásmi), Old Armenian եմ (em), and so on.

4.t: PIE word *h₁én From Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”), cognate with Latin in, Old Armenian ի (i), Albanian një, English in.

8.t: From earlier ἐνς (ens), as attested in Doric, from Proto-Hellenic *en-s, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”), from which also ἐν (en, “in, at, on”).

21.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *eks, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs (“out of”). Cognates include Latin ex, ē, Old Irish ess-, a, ass (Irish as), Lithuanian i̇̀š, Old Church Slavonic из (iz), Northern Kurdish ji, Albanian ith.

56.t: Disputed. * Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ergʰ- (“to move, go”), cognate with ὀρχέομαι (orkhéomai), Albanian erdha (“I came”), Old Irish regaid (“will go”, future of téit), Sanskrit ऋघायति (ṛghāyáti, “to be passionate”). * Alternatively, from…

67.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hodós, possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *sodós (“course”), which is traditionally derived from *sed- (“to sit”) and directly cognate with Proto-Slavic *xodъ (“motion; passage”), with more distant cognates including Sanskrit सा॒द…

39.t: From Proto-Indo-European *kʷís (“who, what”). Cognates include Latin quis and Hittite 𒆪𒅖 (kuiš).

57.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hens, *hmia, from Proto-Indo-European *sḗm, *smih₂. Cognates include Sanskrit सकृत् (sakṛt) and Latin semper.

71.t: From Proto-Indo-European *peri (“in crossing; in passing”), locative singular of *per- (“before; in front”). Cognates include Sanskrit परि॑ (pári), Latin per, Lithuanian per, English for, and Albanian për.

61.t: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yəhūḏā́) and -ς (-s, declension suffix).

32.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kətá, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥-th₂, from *ḱóm (“beside, with”).

25.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mḗ, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₁ (prohibitive particle). Cognate with Old Armenian մի (mi), Sanskrit मा (mā́), Old Persian 𐎶𐎠 (m-a /⁠mā⁠/), and Albanian mos.

24.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *hós, from Proto-Indo-European *Hyós, *Hyéh₂, *Hyód (“who, which”), from the relative stem *Hyo-, possibly from the anaphoric stem *(h₁)i-, *(h₁)e-.

35.t: From Proto-Hellenic *lāwós, with further origin uncertain: * Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂wos (“people (under arms)”), from *leh₂w- (“military action”); in this case, cognate with Phrygian λαϝαγταει (lawagtaei, “military leader”), Hittite 𒆷𒄴𒄩𒀸…

34.t: From ϝοῖκος (woîkos), from Proto-Hellenic *wóikos, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyḱos (“settlement”).

97.t: From earlier *θύγατηρ (*thúgatēr) (compare with the Homeric accusative form θύγατρα (thúgatra) created to avoid the four syllables of θυγατέρα (thugatéra) and fit the hexameter) via Limitation Law which required the accent to be placed on the last two…

33.t: From Proto-Hellenic *dídōmi, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, reduplicated athematic present of *deh₃- (“to give”).

18.t: From Proto-Hellenic *eweikʷon, dissimilated from *eweukʷon, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éwewkʷom, from *wekʷ- (“to speak, make a sound”), from which also came ὄψ (óps, “voice, word”).

19.t: Originally the neuter accusative singular of ὅστις (hóstĭs, “whoever; whichever; whatever”, indefinite relative pronoun), lexicalised as a conjunction.

16.t: Synchronically analyzable as ὁ (ho, “self; third-person pronoun”) + αὐτός (autós, “self; third-person pronoun”).

64.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *ihereús. Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀂𐀋𐀩𐀄 (i-je-re-u).

86.t: Either from ὄρνυμι (órnumi, “I raise”), or possibly directly from a Proto-Indo-European *h₃eros; either way, derived from the root *h₃er- (“to rise, spring, stir”). Compare Sanskrit ऋ॒ष्व (ṛṣvá).

47.t: From an earlier *προτιωπον (*protĭōpon, literally “what is opposite to the eyes [of the other]”), analyzed as προτί (protĭ́, “opposite”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”) + -ον (-on, “nominative neuter suffix”); for the first component, see πρός (prós, “towards”).

12.t: Possibly οὐκί (oukí, “not so, never”), from Proto-Hellenic *oyuki, from Proto-Indo-European *(ne) h₂óyu kʷíd (“(not) ever, (not) on your life”). Compare Sanskrit उद् (ud), Old Armenian ոչ (očʻ), and Albanian as.

11.t: First attested in Mycenean Greek as 𐀞𐀯 (pa-si, equivalent to πᾶσι (pâsĭ)).

79.t: From Proto-Hellenic *ékeyenos, from ἐ- (e-, “augment”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₁é) + *ḱe (“deictic particle”) + Proto-Indo-European *h₁enos (“that”) (compare ἔνη (énē)).

46.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hlagʷ-, probably from a Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂gʷ- (“to take, to grasp”), with cognates including Old English læċċan (English latch) and possibly Sanskrit लग् (lag, “to be attached”).

50.t: Uncertain. Perhaps a reduplicated form of Proto-Indo-European *leh₂-, with cognates including Latin lallō, Lithuanian laluoti, German lallen, English loll, and Welsh llolian.

96.t: A noun use of the present participle of ἄρχω (árkhō, “to rule”).

76.t: Back-formation from ἐκεῖνος (ekeînos). This is the regular distal place demonstrative reflex, whereas ἐκεῖθι (ekeîthĭ) is the obsolete extended form.

36.t: PIE word *Hyós From the relative pronoun ὅς (hós) + -ως (-ōs, adverbial suffix).

d: οὕτω ποτ’ ἦν μῦς καὶ γαλῆ

82.t: Uncertain; has been connected to similar particles in other Indo-European languages, especially Latin an and Gothic 𐌰𐌽 (an), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂en.

45.t: Quantitative metathesis of εἰάν (eiắn), itself a univerbation of εἰ (ei) + ἄν (ắn, modal particle).

51.t: From ἰδοῦ (ĭdoû), aorist middle imperative second singular form of ὁράω (horáō, “to see, to find out, to make sure”).

42.t: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

49.t: From πόρος (póros, “way, bridge”) + -εύω (-eúō). From πείρω (peírō, “to pierce, pass through”).

92.t: Contraction of ἕο αὐτοῦ (héo autoû), literally “his self”.

68.t: From Biblical Hebrew מֹשֶׁה (mōšê). The non-Attic diphthong ⟨ωυ⟩ is found in the Septuagint, and was likely of Ionic origin, though was later regularised in disyllabic Μωσῆς (Mōsês) and trisyllabic Μωϋσῆς (Mōüsês).
